text: A SIEM -- Security Information and Event Management -- is the platform a modern SOC is built around. Strip away the vendor marketing, and every real SIEM does four jobs: it centralizes logs from across the environment, correlates events across those sources in real time, alerts when a pattern looks dangerous, and retains the data long enough to investigate it later. Those four jobs, done together, are what separates a SIEM from a folder full of log files.

Centralization means pulling logs from firewalls, servers, endpoints, and applications into one place, so an analyst isn't logging into a dozen different systems to piece together what happened. Correlation is the step that actually finds trouble: combining events across those sources to spot a pattern that no single log, on its own, would ever reveal. Alerting turns a detected pattern into something a human sees -- a prioritized notification, not a buried log line. And retention keeps that data around after the moment passes.

Here's why correlation is the feature that matters most. A firewall logs a port scan from an external IP address -- on its own, noise; this happens constantly. Minutes later, an endpoint agent logs an antivirus alert on a server sitting behind that same firewall. Two separate systems, two separate log entries, easy to miss individually. A SIEM's correlation engine ties them together by source IP and timing into a single incident -- exactly the pattern a human watching either log alone would never catch.

Retention is the part that's easy to undervalue until you need it. Forensic investigations often start days, weeks, or months after an incident actually happened, and the only way to reconstruct a timeline is if the logs are still there. Compliance frameworks like PCI-DSS and HIPAA go further and require organizations to keep certain logs for a defined minimum period, audited and provable, not just convenient to have.

Next lesson digs into how centralization and correlation actually work under the hood: aggregating logs from completely different vendors, normalizing their formats into something comparable, and only then correlating across them.
